note: Feminine, hence ta valise. faire sa valise = to pack. les bagages is the collective, un sac à dos a rucksack, la consigne the left-luggage office.

fr: Il y a un ascenseur ou c'est par l'escalier ?
en: Is there a lift, or is it up the stairs?
note: Masculine: un ascenseur. Old buildings often have none. l'ascenseur est en panne is a sign you will meet.

fr: C'est sur place ou à emporter ?
en: Is that to eat in or take away?
note: What the bakery or café asks you. Answer sur place, or c'est à emporter.

fr: Le service est compris, on laisse juste la monnaie.
en: Service is included, we just leave the change.
note: Included by law, so there's no tipping arithmetic in France. Rounding up or leaving a couple of euros (un pourboire) is a bonus, never an obligation.

fr: Je peux me garer où ?
en: Where can I park?
note: Reflexive: se garer. le parking is the car park, une place the space, l'horodateur the pay-and-display machine. A zone bleue bay is free but timed – you show a disque.

fr: Au secours ! Appelez les pompiers !
en: Help! Call the fire brigade!
note: The shout in a genuine emergency. aidez-moi for anything less. 112 reaches emergency services in English anywhere in France.

fr: Tu as reçu mon mail ?
en: I'll email you before the weekend.
note: French borrows freely and keeps its own pronunciation: un mail, un texto, le week-end, un parking, le shopping. Some have drifted – un smoking is a dinner jacket, un baby-foot table football.

fr: Ma fille a sa propre chambre maintenant.
en: My daughter's got her own room now.
note: son / sa already points back to the subject, so propre only adds emphasis. It agrees with the noun, not the owner: son propre bureau, sa propre voiture.

fr: Il y a eu une coupure de courant pendant l'orage.
en: There was a power cut during the storm.
note: Feminine: une coupure. Rare in France, but the phrase turns up on notices and in the news.

fr: Le ventilateur fait un bruit d'enfer.
en: Can you put the fan on? It's far too hot.
note: Masculine. In speech it's usually le ventilo. Air conditioning (la clim) is rare in French homes, so a fan is what most people reach for.

fr: Les clés sont à l'intérieur de la voiture.
en: The keys are inside the car.
note: Everyday speech just says dans la voiture. à l'intérieur de is for emphasis or contrast with dehors.

fr: Belle-maman nous a apporté un gâteau.
en: Mother-in-law brought us a cake.
note: Warm and slightly jokey, used as a name with no article. Most French people just use her first name.

fr: Beau-papa s'occupe du barbecue, comme d'habitude.
en: Father-in-law's in charge of the barbecue, as usual.
note: Same register as belle-maman. First names are the norm in practice.

fr: Tu veux de la mayonnaise avec tes frites ?
en: Do you want mayonnaise with your chips?
note: Feminine, hence de la mayonnaise. It's the dip that comes with chips.

fr: Attention, j'ai mis du piment dans la sauce.
en: Careful, I've put chilli in the sauce.
note: Masculine: du piment. French home cooking isn't hot – épicé or pimenté = spicy, and le poivre is the pepper on the table.

fr: Passe-moi le seau, je vais laver la voiture.
en: Pass me the bucket, I'm going to wash the car.
note: Masculine: un seau. Same sound as un sceau (a seal) and un saut (a jump).

fr: L'électricité est devenue vraiment chère.
en: Electricity has got really expensive.
note: Feminine – that's why it's devenue chère and not devenu cher. The bill is la facture d'électricité, and EDF is the usual supplier.

fr: On habitait encore à Lyon à ce moment-là.
en: We were still living in Lyon at that point.
note: à ce moment-là points back to a moment already mentioned. The -là is what makes it 'that' rather than 'this'.

fr: J'étais en train de manger quand tu as appelé.
en: I was in the middle of eating when you rang.
note: The imparfait alone already means 'was doing' (je mangeais quand tu as appelé). en train de only adds emphasis on the interruption.

fr: J'ai réparé le vélo moi-même.
en: I mended the bike myself.
note: Stressed pronoun + -même: moi-même, toi-même, lui-même, elle-même, nous-mêmes. Always hyphenated.

fr: Le petit a un an et demi.
en: The little one is one and a half.
note: Age takes avoir, not être. French just bolts et demi onto the number: un kilo et demi, deux heures et demie (feminine noun, so demie).

fr: Mes grands-parents vont à la messe le dimanche.
en: My grandparents go to mass on Sundays.
note: Feminine: la messe. France is largely secular – midnight mass at Christmas is about as ritual as most families get.

fr: Y a plus de courant, toute la rue est dans le noir.
en: There's no power, the whole street's in the dark.
note: Spoken shortcut for il n'y a plus de courant – the il and the ne both vanish. Also heard: une panne d'électricité.

fr: J'ai le mal des transports, arrête-toi cinq minutes.
en: I feel sick, pull over please.
note: avoir envie de + infinitif. avoir mal au cœur is the milder one – to feel queasy.

fr: Le médecin dit que j'ai de la tension.
en: The doctor says I've got high blood pressure.
note: Feminine: de la tension. avoir de la tension already means it's high. la pression is never used for this.

fr: Mon oncle a du diabète depuis longtemps.
en: My uncle's had diabetes for a long time.
note: Masculine: du diabète. For the person, je suis diabétique. depuis + present is how French says 'has had ... for'.

fr: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient déjà partis.
en: By the time I got there, they'd already left.
note: Plus-que-parfait = imparfait of avoir/être + participle: j'avais fait, j'étais allé. Être-verbs still agree: ils étaient partis.

fr: Tonton et tata arrivent demain matin.
en: Uncle and auntie are arriving tomorrow morning.
note: Children's words, and what adults use in front of children: tonton Jean, tata Marie. Otherwise mon oncle, ma tante.

fr: Ma belle-fille est infirmière à Bordeaux.
en: My daughter-in-law is a nurse in Bordeaux.
note: Same word for stepdaughter. Note the missing article before a job: elle est infirmière, not une infirmière.

fr: C'est mon gendre, le mari de ma fille.
en: That's my son-in-law, my daughter's husband.
note: Masculine: mon gendre. beau-fils also works but usually means stepson.

fr: On ne dit plus mademoiselle, c'est madame pour tout le monde.
en: Nobody says mademoiselle any more, it's madame for everyone.
note: Officially dropped from French forms. Use madame for any adult woman, whatever her age or status.

fr: Tu prends un chou-fleur au marché ?
en: Will you get a cauliflower at the market?
note: Masculine: un chou-fleur, plural des choux-fleurs – chou takes an x, fleur an s.

fr: Il me faut une aubergine pour la ratatouille.
en: I need an aubergine for the ratatouille.
note: Feminine: une aubergine. il me faut is the everyday 'I need' – the thing needed is the subject, like ça me plaît.

fr: Je fais des épinards à la crème ce soir.
en: I'm doing creamed spinach tonight.
note: Always plural in French, so des épinards, never de l'épinard.

fr: Il y a des herbes de Provence dans le placard ?
en: Are there any mixed herbs in the cupboard?
note: The all-purpose French spice jar – thyme, rosemary, oregano, savory. For stews you want un bouquet garni instead.

fr: Tu peux fermer le portail en partant ?
en: Can you shut the gate on your way out?
note: Intonation question with tu peux – the everyday spoken request.

fr: La clé tourne mal dans la serrure.
en: The key doesn't turn properly in the lock.
note: la serrure is feminine. 'Fermer à clé' = to lock up.

fr: Passe le balai pendant que je fais la vaisselle.
en: Give the floor a sweep while I do the washing-up.
note: 'Passer le balai' is the set phrase for sweeping, like 'passer l'aspirateur' for hoovering.

fr: On trie les déchets dans le bac jaune.
en: We sort the rubbish into the yellow bin.
note: on = we in speech. Recycling sorting (le tri) is taken seriously in France.

fr: Il y a un interrupteur juste derrière la porte.
en: There's a light switch right behind the door.
note: un shows it's masculine, since l'interrupteur hides the gender.

fr: J'ai pas le moral en ce moment.
en: I'm feeling a bit low at the moment.
note: Spoken French drops the ne. Low spirits live in avoir, like hunger and thirst.

fr: J'ai du mal à respirer depuis ce matin.
en: I've been struggling to breathe since this morning.
note: avoir du mal à + infinitive = to struggle to do something.

fr: Il a une gastro, il reste à la maison.
en: I've had diarrhoea since last night.
note: depuis + present = have had, ongoing. At the chemist 'j'ai mal au ventre' does the job too.

fr: Je manque un peu de fer, d'après le médecin.
en: I go dizzy when I stand up.
note: Always plural: des vertiges. The everyday version is 'j'ai la tête qui tourne'.

fr: C'est pas une blessure grave, il peut marcher.
en: It's not a bad injury, he can walk.
note: une blessure is feminine. In speech people prefer the verb: 'il s'est blessé'.

fr: La douleur est revenue cette nuit.
en: The pain came back in the night.
note: revenir takes être, so the participle agrees: la douleur est revenue. Day to day you just say 'j'ai mal'.

fr: Tu as tout ce dont tu as besoin ?
en: I know what you want, but not what you need.
note: 'What' inside a sentence: ce que before an object verb, ce dont with verbs taking de (avoir besoin de), ce qui when it's the subject – ce qui s'est passé.

fr: On commande un Uber, c'est plus simple.
en: Let's get an Uber, it's easier.
note: 'Commander un Uber' = to order one. The official word is un VTC.

fr: Le compteur d'électricité est dans le couloir.
en: The electricity meter is in the hallway.
note: Same word for the taxi meter and the one at home.

fr: Si j'en prends trois, vous faites un prix ?
en: If I take three, can you do me a deal?
note: Markets, brocantes and vide-greniers only – haggling in a shop isn't done.

fr: Cinquante euros, c'est votre dernier prix ?
en: Fifty euros, is that your best price?
note: The polite haggling line at a flea market.

fr: Cette maison coûte presque un million d'euros.
en: This house costs nearly a million euros.
note: un million takes de before its noun: un million d'euros. There's no separate word between mille and million.

fr: La vieille église est fermée pour travaux.
en: The old church is closed for building work.
note: 'La vieille église' shows the feminine that l'église hides.

fr: J'ai peur de conduire sur l'autoroute.
en: I'm scared of driving on the motorway.
note: Fear lives in avoir. avoir peur de + noun or infinitive: j'ai peur du noir.

fr: Bonjour, vous pouvez mettre le compteur, s'il vous plaît ?
en: Hello, can you put the meter on, please?
note: Taxis are metered by law, though airport runs into Paris are flat-rate.

fr: Je l'ai laissé là où tu m'as dit.
en: I left it where you told me.
note: où doubles as the relative 'where', and covers 'when' after a time word: le jour où.

fr: C'est comme ça, on n'y peut rien.
en: That's just how it is, nothing you can do.
note: The frozen phrase keeps its ne. Said 'on peut rien y faire' just as often.

fr: Il y avait une vingtaine de personnes au marché.
en: There were about twenty people at the market.
note: -aine makes a round number approximate: une dizaine, une vingtaine, une douzaine.

fr: Je vous dois combien pour les deux ?
en: That comes to a hundred and fifty euros altogether.
note: No 'un' before cent or mille. 'Deux cents' takes an -s only with nothing after it.

fr: On habite au quatrième, sans ascenseur.
en: We're on the fourth floor, with no lift.
note: 'Au quatrième' – étage is left out once it's obvious.

fr: C'est la cinquième fois que je t'appelle.
en: This is the fifth time I've rung you.
note: The u in cinquième keeps the hard k sound.

fr: Le train part à six heures moins le quart.
en: The train leaves at quarter to six.
note: moins le quart = quarter to. Going the other way it's 'six heures et quart'.

fr: Les vacances scolaires commencent en février.
en: The school holidays start in February.
note: Months take no capital letter, and 'in February' is en février.

fr: En mai, on a plein de jours fériés.
en: In May we get loads of bank holidays.
note: 'Plein de' is the spoken 'loads of'. May is full of long weekends in France.

fr: On rentre en France début octobre.
en: We're going back to France at the start of October.
note: Present tense covers the near future in speech. 'début octobre' needs no preposition.

fr: Ici, il pleut beaucoup en novembre.
en: It rains a lot here in November.
note: pleuvoir is irregular and only ever comes with il.

fr: Cette place est réservée aux personnes âgées.
en: This seat is reserved for elderly people.
note: Feminine plural agreement: personnes âgées. The respectful term – avoid calling someone 'vieux' to their face.

fr: La femme de ménage vient le mardi matin.
en: The cleaner comes on Tuesday mornings.
note: 'Le mardi' with the article means every Tuesday. 'La nounou' is the childminder.

fr: Vous m'en mettez une livre, s'il vous plaît.
en: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.
note: Still used at markets: une livre = 500 g. Nothing to do with the pound sterling, which is 'une livre sterling'.

fr: La plaque est encore chaude, ne touche pas.
en: The hob's still hot, don't touch it.
note: Often plural for the whole hob: les plaques. Le four = the oven.

fr: Tu as pris les sacs de courses ?
en: Have you got the shopping bags?
note: Bring your own – free plastic bags are banned. 'Un cabas' is the sturdy market bag.

fr: Il faut purger les radiateurs avant l'hiver.
en: The radiator in the living room isn't heating any more.
note: 'Le chauffage' is the heating in general – flats often share the building's.

fr: Le chauffe-eau est tombé en panne hier soir.
en: The water heater broke down last night.
note: Also called 'le ballon d'eau chaude'. 'La chaudière' is the boiler that heats the flat too.

fr: Va chercher tes chaussons, le carrelage est froid.
en: Go and get your slippers, the tiled floor's cold.
note: 'Les pantoufles' is the same thing. Plenty of French homes keep shoes on, so wait and see.

fr: Je me sers de mon téléphone comme réveil.
en: I use my phone as an alarm clock.
note: se servir de is what people say out loud – utiliser is the neutral written verb.

fr: Mets le haut-parleur, tout le monde veut t'entendre.
en: Put it on speaker, everyone wants to hear you.
note: On your end you'd say 'je te mets sur haut-parleur'.

fr: Ça fait vingt ans qu'ils sont mariés.
en: We're celebrating our wedding anniversary tomorrow.
note: 'Anniversaire' on its own means birthday – the wedding one needs the full phrase.

fr: Au péage, on paie par carte.
en: At the toll you pay by card.
note: Impersonal on = 'you' in general. 'Faire le plein' = to fill up, le gazole is diesel, le sans-plomb 95 unleaded.

fr: L'automne dernier, on est allés en Bretagne.
en: Last autumn we went to Brittany.
note: 'L'automne dernier' shows it's masculine. The set is le printemps (au printemps), l'été, l'automne, l'hiver – all the others take en.
